meta.title: The Ideal Goal
meta.content_note: Discusses the partition of India, communal politics and historical rhetoric about minorities. No graphic imagery.
meta.logline: After the Lahore Resolution, the Muslim League's leaders in the United Provinces had to explain Pakistan to Muslims who would never live in it. Episode 5 follows the pamphlets, speeches and private letters: an Islamic state, a 'laboratory', a jumping-off ground for the Muslim world, a quiet readiness to accept a smaller Pakistan, and minorities held as hostages.
meta.source: Venkat Dhulipala, Creating a New Medina: State Power, Islam, and the Quest for Pakistan in Late Colonial North India (Cambridge University Press, 2015), chapter 4; the pamphlets, speeches and archival letters quoted there.
meta.disclaimer: Original animation and music. Narration paraphrases the book; short quotations are attributed. Maps use modern outlines from Natural Earth (public domain) and are approximate for the 1940s. Not affiliated with the author or publisher.

els.text: TANDA · UNITED PROVINCES · 1940

els.title: P. W. RADICE, I.C.S.
lines: Asked the weavers what they hoped
brethren in Pakistan would be able to
take their revenge on the Hindus there.'

els.text: P. W. Radice Papers, MSS Eur F180/80, British Library; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: In 1940 a British district officer named P. W. Radice visited the Muslim handloom weavers of Tanda, a small town in eastern U.P. He asked them a simple question. What did they hope to gain from Pakistan?

These weavers would never live in Pakistan. Their town was hundreds of miles from any Muslim-majority province. Their answer was blunt. If the Hindus annoyed them, their brethren in Pakistan could take revenge on the Hindus there.
Radice wrote two words in his notes. A pleasant prospect.

els.title: Pakistan
els.author: Anis al Din Ahmad Rizvi · Bareilly · 1940

els.text: a month before the Lahore Resolution
an Islamic state: 'khuda ki badshahat'
the kingdom of God

if a thorn lodged itself in the foot
of a black African Muslim, the Chinese
Muslim would instantly blink his eye
Anis al Din Ahmad Rizvi, Pakistan (Bareilly, 1940); via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: Jinnah liked to complain that the word Pakistan appeared nowhere in the Lahore Resolution. Hindus had invented it, he said. But a month before Lahore, in the western U.P. town of Bareilly, an Aligarh graduate named Anis al Din Ahmad Rizvi had already published a treatise. Its title was one word: Pakistan.
lines.say: Jinnah liked to complain that the word Pakistan appeared nowhere in the Lahore Resolution. Hindus had invented it, he said. But a month before Lahore, in the western U.P. town of Bareilly, an Ali-gur graduate named Anis al Din Ahmad Rizvi had already published a treatise. Its title was one word: Pakistan.

lines.text: Rizvi wanted an Islamic state, ruled by the law of God. Its foreign policy would serve the whole Muslim world, bound so tightly, he wrote, that if a thorn pricked the foot of an African Muslim, a Chinese Muslim would blink.

els.text: RIZVI'S THREE STATES
north-west, with western U.P.:
Meerut, Rohilkhand, Aligarh, Agra
east: Bengal and Assam
south: Hyderabad
modern borders shown, for orientation
Rizvi, Pakistan (1940), map; reproduced in Dhulipala, Map 5

lines.text: And he drew a map. Three Muslim states: one in the north-west that reached deep into U.P. itself, taking in Meerut, Rohilkhand, Aligarh and Agra; one in Bengal and Assam; and the princely state of Hyderabad in the south.
lines.say: And he drew a map. Three Muslim states: one in the north-west that reached deep into U.P. itself, taking in Meerut, Rohilkhand, Ali-gur and Agra; one in Bengal and Assam; and the princely state of Hyderabad in the south.

lines.text: Those left outside would be protected the way the weavers of Tanda imagined: by Hindus living inside Pakistan. Rizvi even welcomed exchanges of population. The hostage idea had reached the mofussil before the Resolution was passed.

els.text:
some kind of confederation
will come into being
no exchange of populations
OSS: would settle 'even at the cost of
modifying the demand for Pakistan'
'Now the old man is talking sense'
Indian Annual Register 1940; OSS report 4162.1 (1946); K. H. Khurshid, Memories of Jinnah; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: The man in charge of the League in U.P. was not so sure. Nawab Ismail Khan told Hindus not to worry. There would be no exchange of populations, he said, and the new sovereign states might well join a confederation with the rest of India.
An American intelligence report later called him a moderate, a man who would settle with Congress even at the cost of watering down Pakistan.

Jinnah's secretary recorded a joke told at a film show. What if the Qaid lost his memory, like the hero of Random Harvest, and asked his committee, what is this Pakistan nonsense? Ismail Khan, came the punchline, would say: now the old man is talking sense.

els.title: M. A. JINNAH
lines: The hand of the British government
The one thing alone that matters
is that we are all Musalmans.

els.text: Mahmudabad-Jinnah correspondence, QA Papers; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: Even the Mahmudabads, the richest Muslim family in Awadh, hesitated. They were Shias. Days after Lahore the old Raja wrote to Jinnah asking for safeguards for his sect, and for the Viceroy to step in if Shia rights were threatened.
Jinnah's reply was cold. The British were leaving. The League alone would now do justice between Muslim and Muslim. The one thing alone that matters, he wrote, is that we are all Musalmans.
The Raja wired back that he was ill, that his brain worked like a wireless in bad weather. Within a week the family had fallen into line.

els.text: I say Islamic, not Muslim.
the second Islamic state, after Medina
'a laboratory wherein we may experiment'
prohibition · no usury · zakat
a 'democratic-theocratic State'
Speech to the Bombay Provincial Muslim League, May 1940; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: His son was a different matter. The young Raja of Mahmudabad, whom Jinnah called his nephew, had skipped Lahore. Jinnah made him chairman of the delegation sent out to sell Pakistan to Muslims across India.

In Bombay in May 1940 he told the provincial League what Pakistan was for. The creation of an Islamic state, he said, mark my words, gentlemen, I say Islamic, not Muslim, is our ideal. The first Islamic state had been the Prophet's Medina. Pakistan would be the second, thirteen centuries later: a laboratory, he called it.
lines.say: In Bombay in May 1940 he told the provincial League what Pakistan was for. The creation of an Islamic state, he said, mark my words, gentlemen, I say Islamic, not Muslim, is our ideal. The first Islamic state had been the Prophet's Madeena. Pakistan would be the second, thirteen centuries later: a laboratory, he called it.

lines.text: Its laws would come from Islam, fixed for ever. There would be prohibition, no usury, and zakat. Non-Muslims would share in the blessings of what he called a democratic-theocratic state.

els.title: MAHMUDABAD TO JINNAH
lines: Could not the same be done in other
districts? And then at the Centre?
We have had enough of democratic
yap yapping. Only one man at the head
can work and does the work.

els.text:
the outposts of Islam will go forward,
they will not be withdrawn

one and only one Islamic
Sultanate for all of us
Mahmudabad to Jinnah, QA Papers; Sidq, 11 May 1941; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: And who would run this state? In Muzaffarnagar the district League had been dissolved and a single man put in charge. Mahmudabad wrote to Jinnah: could not the same be done everywhere, and then at the centre? We have had enough, he wrote, of democratic yap yapping.

Nor would Pakistan mean Muslims retreating from India. The outposts of Islam, he said, will go forward. And at Sasaram, in Bihar, he went further still: the world's Muslims wanted one and only one Islamic sultanate for all of them.

els.text:
Pakistan is not the final goal ...
Pakistan is only the jumping off ground.
to the Governor, February 1940: three dominions
minorities on each side guarantee the other
'there would be retaliation'
Sidq, 21 October 1940; Hallett to Linlithgow, 16 February 1940, Linlithgow Papers; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: Chaudhry Khaliquzzaman, the League's strongman in Lucknow, had been a pan-Islamist since his youth, when he went to Turkey with a medical mission during the Balkan Wars. Just as the Prophet created the first Pakistan in Arabia, he told students, the League would create another in India. Pakistan, he declared, was not the final goal, only the jumping off ground.
lines.say: Chaudhry Kha-leek-uz-za-maan, the League's strongman in Luck-now, had been a pan-Islamist since his youth, when he went to Turkey with a medical mission during the Balkan Wars. Just as the Prophet created the first Pakistan in Arabia, he told students, the League would create another in India. Pakistan, he declared, was not the final goal, only the jumping off ground.

lines.text: Weeks before Lahore he laid out a plan to the Governor of U.P. Two Muslim dominions and one Hindu one. Muslims left in the Hindu dominion would be safe because Hindus in the Muslim dominions would be treated the same way. The Governor wrote down how he had put it back to him, bluntly: in other words, there would be retaliation.

els.text: 'TERRITORIAL READJUSTMENTS'
lost: Calcutta, its port, coal and iron
lost: the Ambala division of Punjab

a political remedy ...
also a psychological cure
no reply came
Khaliquzzaman to Jinnah, 7 October 1942; Pathway to Pakistan (1961); via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: But Khaliq was worried about three words in the Lahore Resolution: with territorial readjustments. Reading the 1941 census, he saw what they could mean. Bengal's Hindu-majority west, with Calcutta, its port, its coal and its iron, could be cut away. So could Punjab's eastern districts. Pakistan would be left with flood plains and a sleepy port at Chittagong.

He wrote to Jinnah in October 1942, and he said the quiet part plainly. One basic principle behind Pakistan was keeping hostages in the Muslim provinces against the Muslims in Hindu provinces. Pakistan was a political remedy, and also a psychological cure. Let the Hindus of Punjab and Bengal go, and the cure would fail. Jinnah never replied.

els.text: LAHORE, MARCH 1940
the phrase means claiming 'Delhi and Aligarh'
DELHI, SEPTEMBER 1942
to a US diplomat: a vote only in eastern Bengal
and, yes, without Calcutta
a week later Jinnah repudiates it
US State Dept 845.00/1574, 9 September 1942; S. S. Pirzada, 'The Lahore Resolution 1940' (1970); via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: The phrase had been defended at Lahore by Liaquat Ali Khan. It was not meant to give up any part of Punjab or Bengal, he told the drafting committee, but to claim centres of Muslim culture like Delhi and Aligarh.
lines.say: The phrase had been defended at Lahore by Lee-aa-kut Ali Khan. It was not meant to give up any part of Punjab or Bengal, he told the drafting committee, but to claim centres of Muslim culture like Delhi and Ali-gur.

lines.text: Two years later he told an American diplomat something else. A plebiscite would be held only in eastern Bengal, where Muslims were a clear majority. When the diplomat said that would cost Pakistan Calcutta, Liaquat agreed.
lines.say: Two years later he told an American diplomat something else. A plebiscite would be held only in eastern Bengal, where Muslims were a clear majority. When the diplomat said that would cost Pakistan Calcutta, Lee-aa-kut agreed.

lines.text: A week later Jinnah told the same diplomat that Calcutta would be in Pakistan, and nearly all of Punjab too. Was Liaquat freelancing, or floating a trial balloon for his chief? Dhulipala's point is that a smaller Pakistan was thinkable at the top as early as 1942.
lines.say: A week later Jinnah told the same diplomat that Calcutta would be in Pakistan, and nearly all of Punjab too. Was Lee-aa-kut freelancing, or floating a trial balloon for his chief? Doo-lee-paa-la's point is that a smaller Pakistan was thinkable at the top as early as 1942.

els.text: commissioned by the U.P. League, with leading ulama
convenor: Syed Sulaiman Nadwi
God is sovereign; a Caliph governs
majority rule called 'a rather stupid rule'
council closed to non-Muslims, Shias, Ahmadis
never debated · one copy lost · printed 1957
a source for the ulama's demands in Pakistan
Sandelvi, Islam ka Siyasi Nizam (Azamgarh, 1957), foreword by Abdul Majid Daryabadi; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: Soon after Lahore, Ismail Khan called together leading scholars at the Nadwatul Ulama in Lucknow, among them Sulaiman Nadwi and Abul Ala Mawdudi, to draft a constitution for an Islamic state in Pakistan. A little-known scholar from the Nadwa, Ishaq Sandelvi, was asked for a first draft. He produced more than three hundred pages.
lines.say: Soon after Lahore, Ismail Khan called together leading scholars at the Nadwatul Ulama in Luck-now, among them Su-lay-maan Nud-vee and Abul Ala Mow-doo-dee, to draft a constitution for an Islamic state in Pakistan. A little-known scholar from the Nadwa, Ishaq Sandelvi, was asked for a first draft. He produced more than three hundred pages.

lines.text: In his design God was sovereign and a pious Caliph governed, chosen by scholars and notables rather than the masses. Majority rule, the draft said, was a rather stupid rule. The Caliph could overrule even a unanimous council, and that council was closed to non-Muslims, Shias and Ahmadis.

The committee never met again to debate it. One copy vanished in the post. But Nadwi kept his, and it was printed in 1957. By then Nadwi had moved to Pakistan to advise its Constituent Assembly on an Islamic constitution, and, Dhulipala argues, this draft fed directly into what the ulama asked for.
lines.say: The committee never met again to debate it. One copy vanished in the post. But Nadwi kept his, and it was printed in 1957. By then Nadwi had moved to Pakistan to advise its Constituent Assembly on an Islamic constitution, and, Doo-lee-paa-la argues, this draft fed directly into what the oo-la-maa asked for.

els.text: 'in a democracy, people are counted, not weighed'
Maulvi Musavvir Ali Khan, District League, Badayun
no earthquake, no Great Wall:
the Frontier Mail will still run
U.P. stays out of Pakistan
its Muslims make 'a necessary sacrifice'

the hand amputated
to save the body
els.by: his metaphor for Muslims left behind

els.text: Musavvir Ali Khan, Musalmanan-i-Hind ka Siyasi Nasbul Ain aur Jamhuriyat-i-Hind (Badayun, 1940); via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: On the nineteenth of April 1940 the League held Pakistan Day across India. In Badayun, after Friday prayers, a local lawyer named Musavvir Ali Khan explained the demand in a speech so admired that the district League paid to print it. Its title promised the political ideal goal of India's Muslims.
Democracy, he said, counted people instead of weighing them. Under a single federation Muslims would be outvoted for ever.
To those who wept over a divided motherland he was scornful. No earthquake would split the land and no Great Wall would rise. The Frontier Mail would still run from U.P. to Punjab.

Unlike Rizvi, he now left all of U.P. out of Pakistan. Its Muslims, he admitted, would gain nothing. They would make a necessary sacrifice, like a hand amputated to save the body. And the balance of power, he promised, would keep them safe.

els.text: AZAD MUSLIM CONFERENCE · DELHI
perhaps 50,000 attend
Allah Bakhsh, Premier of Sind:
the east 'ten times more fantastic'
SIKH CONFERENCE · ALIGARH · JUNE 1940
'an ocean of Sikh blood' (Tara Singh)
about 23,000 converts reported
the League answers with a National Guard
Indian Annual Register 1940; U.P. Police Abstracts of Intelligence, 1940; via Dhulipala, ch. 4

lines.text: Pakistan was not only preached in U.P. It was fought over. A month after Lahore, Congress-minded Muslims led by the Deobandi ulama held an Azad Muslim Conference in Delhi. Observers put the crowd at fifty thousand, as large as Lahore's. The Premier of Sind called a Pakistan in the east ten times more fantastic and a hundred times more fragile than one in the west.
lines.say: Pakistan was not only preached in U.P. It was fought over. A month after Lahore, Congress-minded Muslims led by the Day-oh-bun-dee oo-la-maa held an Azad Muslim Conference in Delhi. Observers put the crowd at fifty thousand, as large as Lahore's. The Premier of Sind called a Pakistan in the east ten times more fantastic and a hundred times more fragile than one in the west.

lines.text: Hindu Sabha workers held an anti-Pakistan day. The Akali leader Master Tara Singh told a Lucknow conference that Pakistan would have to pass through an ocean of Sikh blood.
lines.say: Hindu Sabha workers held an anti-Pakistan day. The Akali leader Master Tara Singh told a Luck-now conference that Pakistan would have to pass through an ocean of Sikh blood.

lines.text: In June, at a Sikh conference in Aligarh, police reported a procession a mile long, twenty elephants, and about twenty-three thousand people converting to Sikhism, with thousands of free kirpans handed out. The League began enrolling Muslims in its National Guard. The temperature was rising.
lines.say: In June, at a Sikh conference in Ali-gur, police reported a procession a mile long, twenty elephants, and about twenty-three thousand people converting to Sikhism, with thousands of free kirpans handed out. The League began enrolling Muslims in its National Guard. The temperature was rising.

els.claim:
U.P. Leaguers publicly promised
Pakistan as an Islamic state.
els.by: Mahmudabad, Khaliquzzaman, Rizvi, Musavvir Ali Khan

els.claim:
That promise was the League's
settled policy.
els.by: Jinnah stayed vague; rhetoric is not a programme

els.claim:
A smaller Pakistan was accepted
at the top by 1942.
els.by: Liaquat to a US diplomat; Jinnah repudiated it a week later

els.claim:
Hostage minorities would keep
each other safe.
els.by: In 1947 minorities on both sides were massacred and expelled

lines.text: So what holds up? That U.P.'s League leaders publicly sold Pakistan as an Islamic state: well supported. The speeches and pamphlets survive in their own words.

That this was the League's settled policy: debated. Jinnah himself rarely spoke in such terms, and critics argue that what a party says to rally its base is not the same as a programme for government.

That a smaller Pakistan was accepted at the top as early as 1942: partly supported. An American record backs Khaliquzzaman's suspicion about Liaquat. But Jinnah publicly and privately demanded far more.
lines.say: That a smaller Pakistan was accepted at the top as early as 1942: partly supported. An American record backs Kha-leek-uz-za-maan's suspicion about Lee-aa-kut. But Jinnah publicly and privately demanded far more.

lines.text: And that minorities, held as hostages on each side, would keep each other safe: weak. In 1947 the hostages became the victims, in Punjab and Bengal and beyond.

els.text: Islamic, or Muslim?
1949 · the Objectives Resolution: sovereignty belongs to God
1956 · the Islamic Republic of Pakistan
1973 · Islam the state religion
1980 · a Federal Shariat Court
a 1940 argument that has never been settled
Constitutions of Pakistan, 1956 and 1973; Objectives Resolution, 12 March 1949

lines.text: Mahmudabad's distinction, Islamic, not Muslim, did not stay in 1940. A state for Muslims, or a state run by Islamic law? Pakistan has argued about it ever since.

In 1949 its Assembly declared that sovereignty belongs to God. In 1956 it became an Islamic Republic. In 1973 Islam was made the state religion, and in 1980 a Federal Shariat Court was set up to test laws against Islam.
And far beyond Pakistan, from South Asia to the Middle East, the same question keeps returning: is a state the home of a faith, or of all its citizens? That last observation is ours.

Episode 6 · The Other Medina
Deoband · 1940 – 1945

lines.text: Next time: the ulama who said no. Husain Ahmad Madani and the Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind argued that Muslims and Hindus could share one nation, as the Prophet's Medina once had. Their critique of Pakistan, and the price they paid for it.
lines.say: Next time: the oo-la-maa who said no. Hu-sain Ah-mud Ma-da-nee and the Jamiat Ulama-i-Hind argued that Muslims and Hindus could share one nation, as the Prophet's Madeena once had. Their critique of Pakistan, and the price they paid for it.
